notes.short: “Blessed” six times, over every part of life
notes.about: In Hebrew each of the six clauses in these verses begins with the word “blessed.” Town and country, children, crops and herds, basket and bowl, coming in and going out: the repeated word spreads the blessing over every part of an obedient Israel's life. Verses 16 to 19 answer with “cursed.”

lines.words: You will be blessed in the city
and blessed in the country.
The fruit of your womb will be blessed, as well as the produce of your land and the offspring of your livestock— the calves of your herds and the lambs of your flocks.
Your basket and kneading bowl will be blessed.
You will be blessed when you come in
and blessed when you go out.

original.note: In Hebrew each of the six clauses opens with barukh, “blessed” (twice as “and blessed”); in verses 4 and 5 the BSB puts the word later in the sentence.

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives these verses as an example of Anaphora, and says verses 16 to 19 repeat “cursed” at the start of each sentence in the same way. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the fulness of God's blessing in all of life is pictured by the sixfold repetition of “blessed”; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) says its six repetitions bring in the forms the blessing would take.

cites.quote: See the same figure in verses 16-19 with the word “ cursed ” repeated at the beginning of successive sentences.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: In Deu 28:3-6, the fulness of the blessing of God in all the relations of life is depicted in a sixfold repetition of the word "blessed." Israel will be blessed in the town and in the field, the two spheres in which its life moves
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The Blessing. The six repetitions of the word "blessed" introduce the particular forms which the blessing would take in the various relations of life.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: The basket and bowl stand for what they hold
notes.about: The blessing is spoken over a basket and a kneading bowl, but the vessels stand for what fills them: the basket for the seed or the fruit gathered in it, and the bowl for the meal, or all that is stored and made ready to eat. On one reading the pair spans the work from first to last.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.part: of the Subject: the container for the contents
figure.means: what the vessels hold: the seed or the fruit gathered in the basket, and the meal or store kept in the bowl

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Subject, the container put for its contents, and takes the basket, probably, for the seed and the kneading trough for the meal, the start and finish of their work. Clarke takes the basket for the olive gathering and vintage it was used to collect, and the store for all that is laid up or made ready to eat.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the basket held, seed or gathered fruit, and some take the two as the very vessels, used to carry things on a journey.

cites.quote: The container is put for the contents. Here, probably, the “basket” is put for the seed, and “kneading-trough” for the meal; the beginning and the end of their labours.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Thy basket - Thy olive gathering and vintage, as the basket was employed to collect those fruits. Store - משארת mishereth, kneading-trough, or remainder; all that is laid up for future use, as well as what is prepared for present consumption.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Moses calls on the heavens and earth to listen
notes.about: Moses opens his song by turning from the people to call on the heavens and the earth to listen. The call marks how weighty the song is. Many read them as called to stand witness, as Moses said he would “call heaven and earth to witness against them” (31:28). Isaiah 1:2 opens the same way.

figure.name: Apostrophe
figure.words: Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; hear, O earth
figure.means: Moses turns from the people to address the heavens and the earth as if they could hear, to mark how weighty his song is

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Apostrophe to inanimate things, the song's solemn opening. Calvin says Moses turns to address heaven and earth as witnesses, though they lack understanding, as Isaiah does. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says Moses summons them to hearken; T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes) says they are invoked to show the weight of what follows; Henry calls it a solemn appeal, as in 31:28.
notes.limit: Some take the heavens and the earth to stand for those who live in them, angels and men; others take them as the heavens and the earth themselves, called to listen as witnesses.

cites.quote: Thus solemnly and emphatically opens this “Song of Moses” (which describes the whole history of Israel from the beginning to the end) and call us to give our attention to it and to consider it.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: heaven and earth would be witnesses of their prodigious obtuseness; nay, he turns and addresses himself to heaven and earth, and thus signifies that it was worthy of the attention of all creatures, even although they were without intelligence or feeling ... just as Isaiah ... in like manner appeals to the heavens and the earth
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Moses summons heaven and earth to hearken to his words, because the instruction which he was about to proclaim concerned both heaven and earth, i.e., the whole universe.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Heaven and earth are here invoked, as elsewhere (see the marginal references), in order to impress on the hearers the importance of what is to follow.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: With a solemn appeal to heaven and earth concerning the truth and importance of what he was about to say ... that he would in this song call heaven and earth to record against them. Heaven and earth would sooner hear than this perverse and unthinking people
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Walls “up to the heavens”: very high walls
notes.about: The people repeat the spies' report of cities “with walls up to the heavens.” The words say more than is literally meant, to stress how high the walls stood. Moses uses the same picture in 9:1, so the walls were truly great; but told this way, the report made the people's hearts melt.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.means: walls of great height, too high, it seemed, to be taken

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Hyperbole, as expressing the cities' great height. Benson calls them a hyperbole for very high walls, which Moses grants in 9:1; Henry, a hyperbole the spies used to dishearten the people.
notes.limit: Some do not take the words as an overstatement but as a true account of how high the towns looked to those who saw them.

cites.quote: “The cities are great, and walled up to heaven,” to express their great height. So Deu 9:1, etc.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The cities are great, and walled up to heaven An hyperbole, signifying that their cities were fenced with very high walls, which Moses himself allows to be true, Deu 9:1.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: as if it were in vain to think of attacking them either by battle, "for the people are taller than we," or by siege, "for the cities are walled up to heaven," an hyperbole which they made use of to serve their ill purpose, which was to dishearten the people
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Two lines, one act: God shares out the nations
notes.about: The second line says the first again and makes it plainer. The Most High giving the nations their inheritance and His dividing the sons of man are one act told twice: He shared out the peoples of the earth.

lines.words: When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance,
when He divided the sons of man,

notes.evidence: Calvin says Moses here says one thing twice, the second clause explaining the first: God shared out the nations as an inheritance is shared, and this is repeated more clearly when the sons of Adam are said to be separated. He prefers this to reading the first line as God dividing the earth among the nations, which he does not reject.
notes.limit: The first line is read two ways: God giving the nations their lands, or God sharing out the nations themselves, as an inheritance is shared. Read the second way, it comes closer still to the second line.

cites.quote: In the word בהנחל, behanchel, there is some ambiguity ... for Moses says the same thing twice over, and the second clause is the explanation of the first. He says, therefore, that God distributed the nations, as an inheritance is divided; and then this is more clearly repeated, when he mentions the separation of the sons of Adam.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The LORD's care pictured by an eagle and its young
notes.about: Moses likens the LORD's care for Israel to an eagle that stirs up its nest and hovers over its young; the rest of the verse can be read of the LORD Himself, spreading His wings and carrying them. The picture shows God rousing, guarding and training His people, as an eagle trains its young to fly.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young
figure.means: the LORD's loving care for Israel: rousing, guarding and training His people, and bearing them up as an eagle does its young

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says Moses describes the Lord's care under the figure of an eagle teaching its young to fly, the point of comparison being the loving care with which He trained Israel. Matthew Henry calls it a similitude first touched in Exodus 19:4 and here enlarged. John Calvin says God compares Himself to an eagle; Joseph Benson, that God's care over Israel is well shown by it.
notes.limit: Some writers read the whole verse as the eagle's acts and verse 12 as the LORD's; one takes the second half of the verse as the LORD's own acts, as it reads here.

cites.quote: Under the figure of an eagle, which teaches its young to fly ... Moses describes the care with which the Lord came to the relief of His people in their helplessness ... The point of comparison between the conduct of God towards Jacob and the acts of an eagle towards its young, is the loving care with which He trained Israel to independence.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He did that for them which the eagle does for her nest of young ones ... The similitude was touched ... I bore you on eagles' wings; here it is enlarged upon. The eagle is observed to have a strong affection for her young, and to show it ... by educating them and teaching them to fly. ... God did thus by Israel
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Two similitudes follow, to express God's love, mingled with solicitude more than paternal. ... Secondly, God compares Himself to an eagle, which not only fosters her young ones under her outspread wings, but also indulgently, and with maternal tenderness tempts them to fly.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The eagle is observed by naturalists to have a most tender affection to her young, and therefore the care of God over Israel is here well illustrated thereby. By her voice she encourages and stirs them up to fly, hovers over them, bears, and defends them by her strength
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words. Enraging God answers provoking His jealousy, and the abominations answer the foreign gods: the abominations spoken of here are idols.

lines.words: They provoked His jealousy with foreign gods;
they enraged Him with abominations.

original.note: In Hebrew the second line runs in reverse order, “with abominations” first and the verb last, so the words go out and come back: jealousy, foreign gods, abominations, anger.

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets the verse out as an introverted parallel, jealousy and anger on the outside and strange gods and abominations within, and says this shows that when abominations are spoken of, idols are meant.

cites.quote: a “They provoked Him to jealousy b with strange gods: b with abominations a provoked they Him to anger.” This shows that when “abominations” are spoken of, idols are meant.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Jealousy and anger, “not God” and idols, in turn
notes.about: Four parts take turns. Provoking God's jealousy in the first answers enraging Him in the third, and that which is not God in the second answers their worthless idols in the fourth.

lines.words: They have provoked My jealousy
by that which is not God;
they have enraged Me
with their worthless idols.

notes.evidence: Bullinger gives the verse as an alternate parallel: the a lines move God to jealousy and to anger, and the b lines name what they did it with, that which is not God and their vanities.

cites.quote: a “They have moved me to jealousy b with that which is not God: a They have provoked me to anger b with their vanities:
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “I am He”, then plainly: “no God besides Me”
notes.about: The second line explains the first. “I am He” leaves the word God unsaid, and the next line says it outright: there is no God besides Me. The LORD calls His people to acknowledge Him as the only true God.

lines.words: See now that I am He;
there is no God besides Me.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line has no word for God; the second line supplies it, elohim.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the word God is left out of the first line because the thought already holds it, and because the parallel line that follows states it clearly. He reads the verse as a demand that Israel acknowledge the LORD as the only true God.

cites.quote: The appeal to their own experience of the worthlessness of idols is followed by a demand that they should acknowledge Jehovah as the only true God. ... The predicate Elohim (vid., Sa2 7:28 ; Isa 37:16 ) is omitted, because it is contained in the thought itself, and moreover is clearly expressed in the parallel clause which follows, "there is not a God beside Me."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Arrows and sword, then blood and heads, in turn
notes.about: Four lines take turns. The third line goes back to the first, the arrows made drunk with blood. The fourth goes back to the second, the sword that devours flesh.

lines.words: I will make My arrows drunk with blood,
while My sword devours flesh
the blood of the slain and captives,
the heads of the enemy leaders.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse as one of two four-line passages whose latter lines are to be referred in turn to the former. Bullinger, under Alternate: the a lines relate to the arrows, the b lines to the sword.

cites.quote: Those which consist of four lines generally form two regular distichs; but there is sometimes a peculiar artifice to be perceived in the distribution of the sentences ... In both the above passages, the latter members are to be alternately referred to the former.
cites.read: the 1816 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/lecturesonsacred02lowt

cites.quote: Here a and a relate to the arrows, while b and b refer to the sword.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Sun and seasons: one harvest said twice
notes.about: The second line says the first again. Both lines speak of the fruits of the earth that the sun and the moon ripen, and the two can hardly be told apart. The word the BSB renders seasons answers the sun in the line before.

lines.words: with the bountiful harvest from the sun
and the abundant yield of the seasons,

original.note: In Hebrew “seasons” is yerachim, the plural of a word for a month, the moon's round. Set against the sun, shemesh, in the line before, it can be read as the moon's changing phases rather than months.

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the produce of the sun and the produce of the moons are both the fruits of the earth, ripened by sun and moon, and that the two can hardly be split into crops that ripen once a year and crops that come more often. He takes the plural moons, in parallel with the sun, as the moon's phases, not months.
notes.limit: Some take the two lines as two kinds of crop: those that ripen once a year, and those that come up several times a year.

cites.quote: The "productions of the sun," ... "the produce of the moons," are the fruits of the earth, which are matured by the influence of the sun and moon ... we can hardly so distinguish the one from the other as to understand by the former the fruits which ripen only once a year ... The plural "moons" in parallelism with the sun does not mean months ... but the different phases which the moon shows
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Journeys out and tents at home, side by side
notes.about: The two lines are built alike: each calls a tribe to rejoice and names where, Zebulun in his journeys and Issachar in his tents. Together they take in life abroad and at home. Some read the pair as one call to both tribes to rejoice in their labour and in their rest.

lines.words: Rejoice, Zebulun, in your journeys,
and Issachar, in your tents.

original.note: In Hebrew the first line's journeys are a going out (yatsa), answered in the second by the tents (ohel).

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the tents answer the going out, two sides of life, work and rest; the parallelism of the lines gives one to Zebulun and the other to Issachar, the whole applying to both. Adam Clarke: as Zebulun prospers in his sea trade, so Issachar in his tents. John Calvin: the verse compares two unlike tribes, Zebulun glad in its expeditions, Issachar in its rest.
notes.limit: The writers differ on whether each line belongs only to its own tribe, Zebulun at sea and Issachar on the land, or whether the pair speaks of both tribes at work and at rest.

cites.quote: "At thy tents" corresponds to "at thy going out" ... and describes in its two aspects of work and production, rest and recreation. Although "going out" ... is attributed to Zebulun, and "remaining in tents" ... to Issachar, ... this is to be attributed to the poetical parallelism of the clauses, and the whole is to be understood as applying to both
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: And, Issachar, in thy tents - That is, as Zebulun should be prosperous in his shipping and traffic, so should Issachar be in his tents - his agriculture and pasturage.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He compares two tribes with each other, which, although neighbors in position, were still very dissimilar; for the one being devoted to mercantile pursuits, went forth frequently in various directions; the other took more delight in quietude and repose; and this their great variety of condition is indicated, when he bids Zebulun rejoice in its expeditions, and Issachar in its domestic repose.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)
